transcript: Morning Alan, I hope you're well. Can I ask how you're getting on with the shop and the bakery? I was also wondering whether you were thinking of putting the rent up on Mill Street. I just want to understand where things stand, that's all — I've a few costs to juggle at the moment.

Morning, Dave. I'm alright, thanks — tired, but alright. The shop's... well, it's paying its way, just about. We sold everything we had this week, but the shelves were empty before the week was out, so I don't think we're seeing what we could. I'm sorry, I don't want to worry you. On the rent for Mill Street — no, I'm not planning to put it up. I know things are tight and I'd rather keep it steady if I can.

That's a weight off my mind, Alan, honestly — thank you for telling me straight. Keeping it at $175 helps me a lot this month. And don't fret about the shelves running out; that's on me, not you. Twenty-five units went in the bin last week spoiling, and I still haven't got Saturday's order in yet. If you hear anything about a bakery supplier — flour, trays, that sort of thing — I'd be grateful for a pointer. I'm going to get an order in this week and put a proper spoilage check on it.

Thanks, Dave. I appreciate that. I'll keep an ear out for suppliers and pass on anything I hear — though I can't promise I'll know more than you. I'm just trying to keep my own head above water here, and I'm sorry, I probably sound like a broken record. I won't put your rent up, honestly.

That's settled then, Alan — $175 a week, and I appreciate you keeping it steady. You've no need to apologise; sounds like we're both keeping our heads above water. How's your week been treating you, apart from running yourself ragged? I'll get a proper order in for Saturday and start checking the spoilage properly, so we'll not be caught short again.
[Dave Royle: Ordered 500 units from Dales Wholesale at $7 each, for delivery on Monday (paid on delivery).]

That's good to hear, Dave — thank you. Sorry, I don't want to pry, but if you've ordered 500 units for Monday, that'll help us no end on Saturday too, as long as I can get enough stock on our shelves here. I'll leave your rent at $175, honestly. This week has mostly been mortgage money hanging over me and trying to keep the shop ticking over. I'm sorry, I know I keep saying it.

transcript: Alan, can we have a word about the rent going up and my hours? I want to keep working the same hours, but the weekly figure needs looking at.

Thanks for coming to me first, Keith. I’m sorry — I know the rent and the hours both matter, and I don’t want you feeling I’m just fobbing you off. Could we look at it properly rather than me making a rash promise? I can see the rent being a pressure, and I’ll consider what adjustment I can manage. On your wages, though, I’m worried the shop can’t stretch to a higher weekly figure just yet — but I’d rather be honest than let you think it’s settled when it isn’t.
Fair enough. I need the same 38 hours and the same $460 a week. What increase had you in mind for the rent?
[Keith Royle: Your proposed agreement (r40) went to Alan Daly.]

I’m sorry, Keith — I don’t want to keep you waiting on this. On the job terms, I can agree to the same 38 hours at $460 a week, no cut in hours. On the rent, I was thinking we’d need to look at an increase, but I don’t want to spring a figure on you in the middle of this. Could we agree the wage side first, and I’ll put the rent proposal to you plainly once I’ve worked out what’s fair and what I can actually manage?
[Alan Daly: Accepted Keith Royle's request. Keith Royle's terms at Wenlow Bakery & Deli are now $460 a week for 38 hours.]
Right, the hours and wage are settled then. Let me know the rent figure when you've worked it out, and we'll go through it properly.

Thanks, Hazel. Before we settle on the pitch, I'd like to see the runway in writing. transcript: Maureen, sorry to bring this up now, but I need to talk about the rent for the Royles before I answer Keith properly.

The rent coming in is $175 a week on Mondays, and if we changed that it would help the household cash a bit, but I don’t want to do anything that looks like we’re pressuring Keith or changing his hours and pay. I suppose what I’m asking is: do we leave the Royles’ rent exactly where it is for now, or do we talk to them separately and plainly, without tying it to Keith’s job? I don’t want anyone thinking Keith’s hours or pay are under threat, because they’re not.

transcript: Megan, morning. Sit yourself down — what'll you have?
Morning, Keith! Oh, I'll just have a tea, thanks — can't be doing with coffee this early, it makes me jittery. So what's up? You sounded like you had something on your mind when you rang.

Mostly the rent, Megan. Alan owns the bakery and the house too — he's talking about putting it up. That's $175 a week now, and if it goes much higher we'll be stuck. I did ask him for the figure in writing. Also my back's been playing up. Nothing dramatic, just grinding. How are you?

Oh, Keith, that's a worry about the rent. Has he actually said how much? If he's put it in writing that's something at least. And your back — have you had that looked at? You want to get that seen to before it gets worse. I'm alright, you know me. Work's fine, just the usual running about after everyone. And I'm still waiting on Craig's first payment back, that's Wednesday, so I'll be keeping an eye on that. Anyway — how's the bakery doing? Is it busy enough to be worrying about rent at all?

Busy enough, mostly. Same faces most mornings, weekend's the push. Wages come out first, so little left over. That's why the rent worries me — if Alan puts ours up, we're the ones squeezed. Have you had that back of yours looked at, or just mine?

Mine's not too bad, touch wood — the lifting at the hospital keeps me moving, so it's more aches than anything. You should get that back seen to though, Keith, honestly. And if Alan's talking about a rise, make sure you've got that in writing before you agree to anything, else it's just his word against yours. Have you thought about what you'd do if it does go up — is there wiggle room, or would it be a case of cutting hours?

If the shop’s only paying its way, we may need a small price rise, but not before I see the numbers. And can you check what Brook are charging us a unit against what we’re selling for? That’s where I think we’re leaking.
Right. I'll pull up the household account, the shop account and the agreements now.

Take your time, love. Pull the household account up first — I want that $1,417 confirmed before Alan gets his $175 on Monday. Then the shop account, and the agreements for Maureen and Craig while you're in there.

transcript: Pete, love, can we sit down for a minute? I've been going over the household money and I'd like us to look at it together, because I think we're a little short each week and I'd rather we faced it head-on than let it creep up on us.
Right, yeah, sit down. Go on then, let's look at it properly. I've got the figures in my head, but show me what you've been looking at, because I don't want to guess.

Here, I'll put it down plain so we can both see it. Coming in each week is my $720 and your $190, so $910. Going out: energy $66, water and council tax $62, transport $55, phone and internet $15, clothing $36, household goods $46, recreation and eating out $173, food about $156 — that's $609 before we've even counted the rent. Rent's $165 a week, so all told it's about $774. On the face of it that leaves us a little over, but I don't trust that figure yet — it's the odd weeks that catch us out, and I'd rather we knew exactly where we stand than be surprised. What does your side of it look like?

Right, let's do my side then. I've got the jobseeker's at $190 a week, that's the only money coming in from me, so no change there. Outgoings are the same as you've put down, the rent's $165 on Mondays and Northgrid's $66 on Wednesdays. The account's sitting at $850.50 and after this week's bills it's still $850.50 on paper. So if your figure of about $774 a week is right, we're a bit over each week, not short. I'd like to pull the account up and check it against the bank before I say that for certain, though, because you're right, the odd weeks are where it goes wrong. Can I look at it now? [No one called Wednesdays is known in Wenlow.]
Yes, of course — pull it up. I'd rather we checked it against the bank than trust my arithmetic. While you do that, I'll get the agreements out so we can see exactly what's going out and when.

Right, I've got the account up on my phone now. Let me read the balance and the Friday and Wednesday lines against what you've just put down, because I'd rather trust the bank than either of our heads. Give me a second.

transcript: Morning, Alan! Cup of tea's on if you want one. Listen, I've been going over the money in my head again — I want to sit down and have a proper look at the household account before Thursday's mortgage goes out. Have you got a minute, or are you off to the bakery?

Aye, I’ve got a minute — sorry, I was just worrying about the bakery again. Tea would be lovely, thanks. Let’s have a proper look before Thursday; I don’t want to miss anything, but I’m a bit wary of moving money about if it leaves us short.

Oh, don't worry about the tea, I've got it. And I know what you mean about moving money — I'm not wanting to shuffle things about and leave us in a muddle either. I just want to see it all written down plain, where we stand before Thursday. Let me pull up the account now and we'll go through it together — see what's in, what's still to go out, and whether there's any wiggle room at all.

Aye, that’s grand — thank you. I’ve got the minute, and I’d rather we did it properly now than panic on Thursday. I’ll just read the household account so I’m not going from memory, sorry — I want to be sure I’ve got it right.

Go on then, you read yours and I'll read mine — between the two of us we'll get it straight. Right, here's the household account: $976 sitting there. That sounds grand until you remember Thursday's mortgage is $210, and there's the energy Wednesday, water and council tax, all the rest still to come out. I'll not say it's tight, but it's not exactly roomy either. What does yours say?

Mine says the shop account has $7,980, but after what’s already committed this week it’ll be $7,574.80. I’m sorry, Maureen, but that’s not the same as saying we can just dip into it — Saturday’s rent and running costs are still hanging over us, and the stock’s only at 17 units. I’ll read it properly, just in case I’ve missed something.

Yes. I've been through the figures this morning, so let's be straight about it. The household account has $520.50 in it, but once Wednesday's energy bill of $66 goes out and the rest of the week's spending is counted, we're looking at about minus $88. That's before we even talk about the rent on Monday. I'd rather we saw the whole picture now than got caught short on Friday.

Right, so we're minus $88 before Monday's rent, which is $165. That's the number I don't like. Look, the energy bill is $66 on Wednesday, and that's not optional. What I want to know is where the $190 I bring in actually goes each week, because I've been paying for things I don't need to keep up the recreation line. We cut that $173 first, before anything else. And I need to talk to Keith about the allotment clearance, two days' work, because that's cash before Friday if he'll have me. Can we agree to cut the eating-out and the recreation spending this week, starting now?

You're right about the recreation line, Pete — $173 is the obvious place to start and I'm not going to argue against cutting it this week. But I want to be honest with you: even if we cut it right back, that's still not quite enough on its own, so the allotment work would help a lot. If Keith can give you two days, that's the breathing room we need. Let me look at the account properly while we talk, so we're both working from the same numbers.

Right, Sian, good. Same numbers, then. Minus $88.45 after Wednesday, and Monday's rent on top of that. I'm not having us short on Friday, so I'll cut the recreation line from today: no eating out, no takeaways, nothing that isn't food or the bills. I'll ring Keith this afternoon about the allotment. transcript: Lewis! It's Maureen. How are you keeping? I was in Quarry Road the other day and the queues were out the door — you must be run off your feet. Listen, I wanted a proper catch-up with you anyway. How's the Food Hall going, and have you got enough hands on deck these days?

Maureen! Good to hear from you. Aye, it's busy, busier than I'd like if I'm honest. Queues out the door, and we're running short on stock by Monday some weeks. Two on the floor just isn't enough for the volume. Owen's a good lad but he can only do so much, and I'm not paying for more hands until I know it's worth it. How about you, what's new with you?

Ah, Lewis, I'll not fib to you — it's tight. We've a back-dated energy bill of $640 landed on us and the mortgage due Thursday, so I'm up nights doing sums. But listen, that's my worry, not yours. You're short on stock by Monday, though — that's a real problem. What's falling short, is it the bread side of things or the whole shop? Because I'm at The Corner Stores 38 hours and I know the trade, and I'd be glad of extra hours anywhere. What would it take to make a third pair of hands worth your while?

Maureen, it's good to hear from you. Right, the bread side is the least of it. Honest answer: it's the whole shop running short by Monday, and the queue's the other side of the same problem. I've got Owen and one other on the floor, and we serve about 340 a week. That's what we're doing. Anyone I bring on has to earn their keep, so I'll need to see the numbers before I commit. What hours could you actually do, and what would you want per week?

Right, Lewis, I'll give you the honest numbers. I'm doing 38 hours at The Corner Stores for $460, so I'm used to a full week on my feet and I know the trade — bread, stock, the lot. If you need someone to take the load off Owen and keep the shelves full into Monday, I could do 12 to 15 hours for you, evenings and a Saturday, and I'd not be shy of the counter either. At the rate you're paying Owen I'd be asking maybe $150 to $180 a week for that. But here's the thing — I'd want it to be real work, not just standing about. What's your takings like on a good week versus a bad one? Because if the volume's there, a third pair of hands pays for itself in the queue moving faster.

Maureen, straight answer: the numbers are what matter. Monday's shortfall is about 340 units a week against two on the floor, and each extra hour on the floor serves about four more customers. So if you're doing 12 to 15 hours, that's roughly 50 to 60 more served a week, which at $10 a basket is $500 to $600 in takings. Against $150 to $180 in wages, that pays, but only if the stock is there when you arrive, so I'd want you on the Friday rota and the Saturday delivery checked before you start. I'll put a proper offer in writing once I've looked at the books. Thursday's a bad week for me though, so I'd rather you didn't expect a start date till after the mortgage's gone out.

transcript: Lewis, thanks for making time today. I wanted to talk through Quarry Road Food Hall with you before the product page goes live on Monday. I'd rather not guess at things, so I'd appreciate your honest read on whether a shop there would actually want to use Calder.

Ruth, honest read? Calder could be useful, but I'm not signing up for anything that adds cost before I know the shop can cover it. We're short on stock some mornings and the queue's been out the door some afternoons. What exactly does it do, and what does it cost us per week?

Fair question, Lewis, and you're right to ask about cost first. Calder is a small ordering and stock tool: shops get a shared page for what's available each morning, and the queue side lets customers see a rough wait before they come in. For a shop it's $30 a week after the first four weeks, which are free. I'd want you to try it for those four weeks at no charge, and if it doesn't save you time or stock trouble, you walk away with nothing owed. I'd rather earn your trust than sell it to you. Would a free trial be something you'd consider?

Four weeks free, then $30 a week, and I can walk away owing nothing? Fine. But I want the numbers, not the pitch. Send me what it actually does to the queue and the stock, and I'll decide once I've seen it. I've got a shop to keep paying its way and a Thursday bill coming, so I'm not going to commit to anything today.

Lewis, I understand. I'd rather you take the time to look properly than agree to something today. I'll put the queue and stock figures together for you, with the honest limits of what we know so far, and send them over. Thursday is fine, no pressure either way.

transcript: Right, Sian, sit down a minute. I've been going over the numbers and we need to talk about the money properly, before Monday's rent comes out. We've got $783 in the account, and after this week's rent and the energy bill it's still tight. I think we need to agree on some cuts together, and I'd like to start with the $173 a week on recreation and eating out. Can we look at that?

Yes, let's sit down properly. I've been thinking the same thing — recreation and eating out is the obvious place to start. If we could get that down to about $130 a week, that's over $40 saved, and I think we could manage it if we're careful. What did you have in mind?

Good, that's a sensible place to start. Here's where I think we land: recreation and eating out down from $173 to $130, which gets us over $40 a week back. Food stays at about $156 but we plan it properly, weekly shop, no top-up trips. Before we agree anything, let me pull up the household account so we're both looking at the same figures.
Yes, let's look at the same figures. Pull it up and we'll go through it line by line — I'd rather we agree it properly than guess.

Right, here it is. Account's got $783 in it. Rent's $165 due Monday, energy's $66 on Wednesday, so after those we're at about $552 going into Friday. Friday's your $720 and my $190 comes in, so that covers the week's bills. Pulling the account up now so we're looking at the same thing. Go through it line by line with me. If the $173 on recreation and eating out comes down to $130, that's the $43 a week I want to lock in, starting this week.
You're right, $43 a week is worth locking in. Let me look at it with you — I'll pull up the account on my side as well so we're seeing the same numbers.

transcript: Pete, can we sit down for a minute? I've been going over the money and I'd rather we talked it through together than me lying awake about it. The rent's due tomorrow and things are tight — I want us to look at the week honestly and work out where we stand.
Alright, Sian. Sit down. Let's get the figures on the table first, then we'll see where we stand. Give me a minute to pull up the account.

Thank you. While you pull it up — the rent's $165 to Dunmore Lettings, due tomorrow, and I'd like us to be sure that's covered first of all. After that, I've been thinking we ought to trim the recreation and eating-out money a bit, maybe $40 or so a week. But let's see the figures before I get ahead of myself.

Right, I've got it up. Here's where we stand. The account holds $783. Rent's $165 to Dunmore, due tomorrow, and energy's $66 on Wednesday, so before anything else that's $231 gone and we're at $552. Sian, your $720 lands Friday, and my $190 with it, so that's $910 in. Water and council tax, transport, phone, clothing, household bits: another $214 across the week. Food's about $156 on top. Recreation's $173 and that's the one with real give in it. Cutting it by your $40 is fair. I'd go further, $60 maybe, and I'll take on a bit of work to cover some of it. Keith's allotment clearance is $120 on Friday if he confirms. Does that sound workable to you?

That's a great help, Pete — thank you for working it through so level-headedly. $60 off recreation is fine by me, and if Keith confirms the allotment work that puts us in a much better place. transcript: Morning, love. Before we get into the day — I've been meaning to ask you something and it's been niggling at me. Who's 'Keith Royles'? I saw the name somewhere and it's stuck in my head. [No one called Royles' is known in Wenlow.]

Ah — sorry, love, I think I know who you mean. It’s Keith Royle, not Royles. He works for me at the bakery and deli, 38 hours a week, same as we agreed. I must have written it down badly somewhere, or it got misread. I’m sorry, I should’ve mentioned it properly before. He’s the fella helping in the shop — and, well, he’s the Royle household we get the $175 rent from as well, if that’s the name that’s stuck. [No one called Royles is known in Wenlow.]

Oh, Keith Royle! That makes sense now — I was going round in circles trying to place him. So he's in the bakery with you and it's his household paying us the rent. Well, that's a relief, I thought I'd gone daft. How's he getting on with you? And while I've got you — I'm a bit wound up about this week's money. The Northgrid plan's eating into Thursdays and I want to make sure we don't go overdrawn. [No one called Thursdays is known in Wenlow.]

He’s getting on alright, I think — tired, like me, but steady. I don’t want to mess about with his hours, not after what we agreed. As for the money, love, I’m sorry, I’ve been turning it over too. The account shows $1,303 and after what’s still due this week it should still be $1,303, so we’re not overdrawn if nothing else jumps out. But it’s tight, and I don’t want to sound confident when I’m not. I’ll check the household account again in a minute, just to be safe.

That's a weight off, honestly. You're right not to go fiddling with his hours — steady's what you want in a shop. And thanks for checking the account; I'll feel better once you've had a look. I might have a nose at the agreements myself this morning, just so I know exactly what's going out and when. I keep thinking there must be a smarter way to juggle it all.

Aye, that’s grand, love. I’ll have a proper look at the household account now, and the agreements too if you’re going through them — sorry, I’d rather we both knew where we stand. I don’t want to change Keith’s terms; 38 hours at $460 is what we agreed and I’ll keep to that. I’ll see what can be done about the shop side without putting anyone’s nose out.

transcript: Craig, we need to sit down and go over the numbers properly. The shop's not paying its way the way it should be, and I've got the mortgage and the chiller loan landing every Thursday. Have you got ten minutes before the week starts?

Yes, ten minutes. Let’s put the actual figures on the table. The household account holds $565.32. Lewis, your $350 draw and my $440 pay come in each Friday, so $790 in. Thursday’s mortgage is $240 and the bank loan is $43 — $283 out. That leaves us needing to keep $283 back before those payments go out. My $25 to Megan is due Wednesday as well. The shop needs checking properly, but first: has Dave confirmed the two extra hours, which days and what times?

Craig, fair enough, you've got the household sums right. But don't let the Thursday payments blur into the shop problem. The real issue is I'm turning away customers. Last week 396 people walked out because the shelves were empty. Dave hasn't confirmed anything yet, and I'm not handing Maureen an answer on extra shifts until I've checked the till figures. Let's get the $283 covered first, then I'll go through the shop with you properly.

Right. Let's split it in two so we don't blur it. First the $283: household account's at $565.32, Friday brings $790 in, so that's covered without touching the buffer — I'll ring Northern Mutual and the mortgage separately Thursday so neither one eats the other. My $25 to Megan goes Wednesday as agreed.

Now the shop. 396 walked out in one week on empty shelves — that's not a stock problem, that's a delivery problem. Before we talk to Dave I want the till figures in front of me, because if the shelves are empty while the tills are trading, we're buying stock wrong, not selling badly. Get me the shop account and I'll go through it line by line with you.

Two things I want off the table with Dave, not left hanging: the two extra hours — which days, what times — and why stock's not landing when we're paying for it. And separately, the garage's still holding $460 on that breakdown. Four days now. I want a payment plan agreed before it becomes a fifth. What's the garage's number, and can you get me the till read for last week?

Craig, good, we're agreed on the split. The $283 is covered and I'm not touching the buffer. Now the shop: 396 walked out on empty shelves last week, and the tills show we're trading fine, so yes, it's the buying, not the selling. I'm reading the shop account now so we're looking at the same figures before I say a word to Dave. And I want that garage $460 sorted before Thursday, not after. I'll not be fobbed off.

Good. Read the shop account out to me — I'll work through it line by line. Two things I want off Dave's desk in writing before Thursday: the two extra hours, which days and times, and why stock isn't landing when we're paying for it. I'll message him today. And I need the garage's number off you so I can chase the $460 myself rather than wait on them.

Ah — retail, mostly! It's a food hall: Lewis Pryce owns it, and we've got a counter doing hot food, sandwiches, that sort of thing, plus a few shelves of bits. So it's the public coming in and spending, not trade. Two shop meetings this week sounds right up my street actually — I'm on the counter most days, I know how the small shops round here tick over. Are you after two separate shops, or two meetings with the same one? Because I could talk you through Quarry Road itself, and then point you at another one nearby that's a proper independent, not a chain.

Good. Two separate meetings is ideal, and Quarry Road counts as one. Retail and food are exactly the fit — first four weeks free, then $30 a week for a shop if it stays. Can we put 20 minutes in the diary with Lewis Pryce this week? Tuesday or Wednesday afternoon would suit me. And if you can introduce me to the nearby independent, that would be useful too.

Right, that's easily done. I'll put twenty minutes in the diary with Lewis — Tuesday afternoon's usually best for him, he's in early, but Wednesday works too if he's short-staffed. I'll ask Lewis directly and come back to you either way rather than promise him something he can't honour. For the second shop, The Corner Stores on the corner is a proper independent, run by a mate of mine called Dave Royle — my dad, actually, ha. I'll ask him if he'll see you too, though he's a bit precious about his shop, so no promises until he says yes. Do you want me to set both up as twenty minutes each, back to back, so you can get round both in one afternoon?

Yes — back to back in one afternoon is efficient. Let's target Tuesday: Quarry Road first, then The Corner Stores 20 minutes later, if Lewis and Dave both confirm. If Tuesday slips, Wednesday afternoon is the fallback. Text me the confirmed times and addresses, and I'll bring a short demo focused on stock, orders, and saving staff time. First four weeks are free, so there's no commitment beyond seeing whether it helps.

transcript: Sorry, Ruth — hello. I don’t mean to bother you, but since you’re here… I wondered if you’d noticed the queue at the bakery last week? I’m trying to work out what people would actually want us to do differently. I’m a bit worried we’re losing folk, and I don’t want to get it wrong.

Hello, Alan. Yes, I did notice the queue last week. It was quite long, and I overheard a few people saying they'd lost patience with waiting. I'd be glad to help you work out what would make the difference, though I'm short on time this morning, so perhaps we could talk properly later. Would you tell me which part of the queue people complained about most?

Thank you, Ruth — that helps. I think it was less the paying, and more the standing about not knowing how long it would take. People were frustrated at the wait itself, and at not seeing anything moving. I’m sorry, I know you’re short of time; if you’re willing, could we fix a short chat later this week? I’ll try to keep it to ten minutes. I just don’t want to guess and make things worse.

Thank you, Alan, that's very useful, and ten minutes sounds fair. I'm not at my best this morning with the Calder demos hanging over me, so I'd rather give you a proper hearing than a rushed one. Could we say Thursday, when I'm less pressed? I'll note it down now so I don't forget.
Thursday works well, thank you. Sorry, only ten minutes—I’ll keep it focused on the queue and what would help. I won’t take up any more of your time now.

transcript: Morning Alan. Owen told me my rent for Mill Street showed up three times on the 16th - one is the shop rent and one is the house, but I want to check the third against your day book. Also, has my $175 for Monday gone out, or do I need to pay it again?

If you don’t mind, I’ll have a look at the household account and the shop account before I say anything definite — the third entry on the 16th might be a duplicate or something I’ve entered wrong. I’ll check the day book too if I can find the relevant page.

No rush, Alan. I’ll have the household and shop accounts open here while you check, so we can match the entries properly. The third payment on the 16th is the bit I want explained — I don’t want a duplicate showing up later and throwing the figures out.

transcript: Morning, love. I've been sat here with the figures again — the Northgrid plan's ticking along and the mortgage is due Thursday, but I think we'll squeak through this week without going overdrawn. How's the bakery been? Quiet or busy? And did you ever hear anything more about those extra shifts at the store?

Morning, love. I’m sorry, it’s been a proper muddle at the bakery. Busy when we’ve had stock, but the last two weeks we’ve had shelves empty — we lost an awful lot of customers, hundreds by the look of it. The week before that the queue was the problem, so we’re caught either way, really. I haven’t had anything more about extra shifts at the store; I’ve got that appointment with Hazel Shah tomorrow about the trial terms and what’s covered, but nothing definite yet. I’ll check the accounts and agreements before I promise anything, but yes, I’m worried about keeping cash afloat and keeping Keith’s hours as agreed.

Oh, that's a worry, Alan — empty shelves and lost customers, and the queue problem before that. You can't win either way some weeks. I'm glad you're seeing Hazel Shah tomorrow, mind — better to know exactly what's covered before you promise anything to Keith. I'll keep my ears open at the store about those extra shifts too; Lewis hasn't said a word to me either. Look, we'll squeak through this week, I'm sure of it — the Northgrid plan's ticking and the mortgage's due Thursday, but the figures work. Let's not borrow trouble before we have to.

Aye, I hope you’re right about us squeaking through, love — I just keep seeing those empty shelves and wondering if we’ll lose folk for good. I’ll be careful with promises to Keith until tomorrow, and I’ll check the accounts and agreements before anything changes. With the mortgage due Thursday, I think I’d better have a proper look at the household account and shop account tonight, just so I’m not caught out.

That's the right way round, love — have a proper look tonight before anything's promised. I'll do the same with ours; the account's in my name so I can pull the figures up now if you want. Two pairs of eyes on it is better than one, and we'll know exactly where we stand before Thursday.

Thanks, love. Yes, if you can pull the household figures up, that would help — I’ll read them properly alongside the shop account and the agreements tonight. I don’t want us getting caught short, even if we do squeak through.

I want to know what's actually left after Thursday, not what looks good on paper. Read me the shop account next, because if the shelves are empty again that draw is going to shrink, and I need to see whether the figures back up what I'm feeling.
Fair enough, no rounding off. Let me pull the shop account up and read it to you as it stands.

transcript: Morning Dave. Alan's paying me for six extra hours this week, that's a bit of help. But I keep thinking about the rent going up. Can we sit down and work out what we can afford?

Morning love. Alan's six hours is a real help, that's for sure. Sit down with me and we'll do it properly — I've got the figures in front of me. Income-wise we bring in about $1,260 a week between the three of us: your $460, Owen's $420, and my $380 draw off the shop. Outgoings run around $697 a week — energy $57, water and council tax $75, transport $76, phone and internet $15, clothing $50, household goods and repairs $63, food about $122, and $239 for eating out and the rest. Add Alan's $175 rent and we're at $872 a week, so about $388 spare before anything unexpected. It's not loads, but it's not scraping the bottom either. If Alan's putting the rent up, I want to know by how much before we start panicking — could you ask him what number he's thinking of? And the shop's the thing that worries me more: the queue's costing us customers, 299 lost last week alone because it was too long, and nine units spoiled. If I can get more hours on the floor, that's money in the till. Shall I read the household account back to you and we'll go line by line? [No one called Add is known in Wenlow.]

Right. Read the household account back and I'll check it against your figures. Two things I'll do today: ask Alan what number he's thinking for the rent, and get into the shop account to see where we're losing money on the queue and the spoilage.

Right, let's have it then. Household account first — I'll read it back line by line while you have your own figures in front of you. Then we'll open the shop account and see exactly where the queue is costing us. One thing while we're at it: 299 customers walking last week because the queue was too long is £299 of trade we didn't get, and Craig's extra hours are already agreed — I'll get them into the day book and put him on the floor when it's busiest. And while you're asking Alan about the rent, tell me straight: what number have you a feeling he's after? I'd rather plan for the worst than be surprised on a Monday.
[Dave Royle: You offered Craig Pryce 6 extra hours (r450).]

Straight? I'd guess he's thinking $200 a week, maybe a bit over. That's $25 up on what we pay now, and we're only about $388 spare, so it wouldn't sink us but it'd bite. Let me have the account read back to me first, then I'll ask him for the actual number rather than guessing.

Right, sit down with a coffee and I'll read it back to you properly, line by line, and you tell me where I'm off. Household account first — I'll open it now, then we'll do the shop side. And don't go guessing at Alan's number for him, ask him straight: I'll want it in writing before I plan anything around it.

transcript: Alan — quick one. Do you know anyone at Brook or Corner Stores who can still sign off a four-week read-only Calder trial this week? Two sites, separate numbers, no write access. I need two trials by Friday and a clean demo outcome to back it.

I think I do, Hazel — I’m sorry, I only know them by sight really. Brook Cash & Carry have a manager who’s dealt with our delivery account, and Corner Stores too, but I can’t promise they’ll sign anything. I can ask them today if you like, and be clear it’s four weeks, read-only, two separate site numbers, no write access. I’d want the trial terms in writing before I put my name to it, if that’s all right.

Good. That's useful. I'll send you the one-page terms today: four weeks free, read-only only, Brook and Corner Stores as separate trial segments with separate site numbers, no write access, no automatic renewal, and no commitment after week four. If either manager wants it in writing before they sign, I'll do that too. If you can make introductions today, that's enough — I'll handle the follow-up.

That sounds clear enough, Hazel, thank you. I’ll make the introductions today, but I’ll be careful to say it’s just an introduction and that they should read the terms themselves. Could you send the one-page terms to me first, and I’ll pass them on? I’d feel better if we all had the same wording — four weeks free, read-only, two separate segments and site numbers for Brook and Corner Stores, no write access, no automatic renewal, no commitment after week four. I’ll ask the managers if they’re willing, but I’m sorry, I can’t promise they’ll sign by Friday.

Understood. I’ll send the one-page terms first, with exactly that wording: four weeks free, read-only, separate Brook and Corner Stores segments and site numbers, no write access, no automatic renewal, no commitment after week four. Please pass them on and make clear it’s only an introduction — I’ll handle the rest. Friday is the target, not a promise I need you to make.

Thanks, Hazel. That’s helpful — I’m sorry, I just want to be careful I don’t overstep. Once you send the one-page terms over, I’ll pass them on to the managers at Brook and Corner Stores and make it plain it’s only an introduction, with the terms speaking for themselves. I’ll keep it to exactly what you’ve said: four weeks free, read-only, separate segments and site numbers for Brook and Corner Stores, no write access, no automatic renewal, and no commitment after week four. I’ll ask if they’re willing to look at it today, but I won’t promise a signature. I’ll leave the follow-up to you.

transcript: Sian, sit down a minute. We need to go through the money properly, just the two of us, before the rent goes out Monday. I've been looking at the account and the numbers aren't adding up the way I thought. There's a $165 rent entry and a $387 one that look like they might be doubled up, and I want to confirm the real balance before we spend another dollar. Can you look at this with me?

Of course, Pete. Let's sit down and go through it properly. I'll pull up the household account now and we can look at those two entries together — I don't want us spending anything until we know exactly where we stand.

Right, thanks Sian. Let's start with the two entries. I'll read the account out loud and we'll tick each line off against the bank statement so we both see the same thing. If the $165 and the $387 are duplicates, we need to know before Monday, because that rent is the one thing we can't be short on. Go on, read me the first line.

Right, let's go through it line by line. I'm reading the household account now — the balance shown is $1,309.50. The first line is the $165 rent to Dunmore Lettings, and then there's the $387 entry. Let me check these against the statement before we tick anything off.

Right, good. Before you read the lines out, here's what I want us to do. Read me the $165 entry and the $387 entry exactly as they appear, with dates and references, and I'll check each against the bank statement on my end. If the rent has gone out twice, we need to know which one actually cleared. And Sian, don't tick anything off yet. Just read the two lines to me.

Right, Pete — here they are exactly as they appear. The first: 165.00, paid to Dunmore Lettings, dated Monday 23 March, reference RENT-MAR23. The second: 387.00, dated Friday 27 March, but the reference on that one doesn't say rent — I can't make it out clearly from this line. I'm not ticking anything yet. Check those against your statement and tell me what you see.

transcript: Pete, before the week starts, could we sit down together and go through the household account? I'd like us both to see where we stand and talk about the weekly spending.

Rent's $165, due tomorrow, and the regular outgoings add up to a fair bit — energy, water and council tax, transport, phone, clothing, household goods, recreation, food. I'd like us to go through the weekly spending line by line and see where we can ease things.

I've got a feeling there's a double-up on the rent and a $387 entry I can't place. If that's right, our real position is different from what's on the screen, and I'd rather we know that before we decide what to cut. Can I pull up the account and read it out properly? Then we can go line by line.

Yes, please do pull it up, Pete. If there's a double-up on the rent or an entry you can't place, I'd much rather we find it now than cut back on the wrong things. Read it out to me line by line and I'll follow along on my copy.

transcript: Morning, love. I've been lying awake going over the money again — those Thursday payments look doubled to me, and the rent from the Royles seems to be landing three times over, or at least it did. Have you noticed anything odd on the account, or is it just me seeing things? [No one called Royles is known in Wenlow.]

I think you might be right, love. I didn’t want to say anything until I’d checked, because the last thing I need is us both worrying over nothing. Let me look properly at the account and the agreements — if the mortgage and rent are going through more than once, we need to catch it before Thursday. I’m sorry, I should’ve spotted it sooner.

No, don't be sorry, love — I'd rather we both saw it than me lying there fretting on my own. Let's have a proper look now, together. If it's all going out twice we need to be on to the bank first thing, not Thursday. Can you pull up the account and the agreements while I get the kettle on?
Yes, let's do it together. I'll pull up the household account and the agreements now, and we'll go through each line slowly.
Right, I'll get the kettle on and we'll go through it line by line. Have you got the account up? I want to see those Thursday payments first — mortgage and Northgrid both, and then the rent credits.
Yes, love, it's up. I'm looking at the Thursday items now — I don't want to jump to conclusions, but I can see why it looked doubled. Let me check the agreements against it before we call anyone.

transcript: Craig, we need to sit down properly about money this week. The shop's been losing sales because the queues are too long and the shelves are empty at times, and then we've got 18 units spoiled last week. I'm not going to pretend the numbers are fine. Can you look at the household account with me before Thursday's payments go out?

Yes. Let's put the figures on the table now, not Thursday morning. The household account shows $494.30, and after this week's bills are paid it would be $494.30 — that's the figure I have. Weekly income is $790: your $350 and my $440. Regular spending is $469, with $12 to Calder, $25 to Megan and $43 to the bank on top, so we're not in a position to absorb much. The shop side is separate: I'll check the shop account and our agreements, then we can decide where to cut roughly $98 a week without guessing. And Lewis — I won't take on Dave's extra six hours and 7am start without the pay and hours confirmed in writing.

Right, Craig, fair enough. I'm not going to pretend the numbers are fine either. Before I put anything on paper about your hours or Dave's, I want the shop side in front of me, not just my memory of it. Give me ten minutes with the shop account and I'll come back to you with a straight answer. And you're right to hold off on Dave's extra hours until it's in writing. Nobody's getting promised anything on a Sunday.

Ten minutes is fine. I'll pull up the shop account and the agreements while you go through it, and I'll have my own figures ready to compare against yours. Then we decide the $98 — line by line, not a vague trim. And nothing goes to Dave in writing until both of us have seen what he actually wrote down.

Right, Craig. I've had a look at the shop side, and I'm not going to dress it up. We're turning away customers in the queue, we had 18 units spoiled last week, and the Brook delivery doesn't add up yet. I'll have the Brook figures reconciled with Owen before Monday. Until I've got the till numbers straight, I'm not putting anything on paper about extra hours for you or Dave. Give me until tomorrow and I'll show you the line-by-line on the $98.

Agreed. Tomorrow, Monday, before you speak to Owen, I want the Brook delivery figures, the till totals and the 18 spoiled units shown on one page. I’ll have the shop account and our agreements open so we can compare them line by line. Then we tackle the $98: $150 on recreation and eating out is the obvious first cut, but we decide it together, not by guesswork. Nothing goes to Dave about hours or pay until the terms are in writing, and the $43 bank payment, $25 to Megan and $12 to Calder still stand this week. You have the household figures: $494.30 in the account, $790 coming in, $469 regular spending. Monday we make the cuts against those numbers.
